utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. I understand there may be a matter you wish to raise, Mr. Saxon, before the Defence gives its opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, just two procedural points. Last night the Prosecution reviewed the timing of direct examination, cross-examination, and re-direct proposed by my learned colleague. And while the Prosecution is grateful for the proposals of the one-to-one ratio between direct exam and cross-examination, and will do its very best to stick to that ratio if not use less time, the Prosecution is concerned about the timing, the proposed timing, for one particular witness from the Boskoski Defence, and perhaps we should move into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. [Interpretation] Mr. President, Esteemed Judges, it is my duty and honour to address the Trial Chamber on behalf of Mr. Boskoski Defence by presenting this opening statement before the Defence starts presenting its case. Your Honours, it was by no mean easy to choose what issues to raise in this opening statement. It was particularly difficult in light of the fact that the Defence, at this very moment, is convinced that the Prosecutor, in the course of the presentation of their own case, failed to prove a single important element of the indictment. It was even more difficult to decide whether to start presenting our case at all in a situation like this and whether our evidence will help you, Your Honours, to reach a decision in respect of the responsibility of our client. The decision has been made. The Defence will present its case in a very limited scope, so this opening statement will very much go along these same lines. We shall try not to start evaluating the evidence which would go against the meaning of the opening statement. We shall keep our argument and evaluation of all the evidence to the final statement of the Defence. In our opening statement, Your Honours, we shall refer briefly to the burden of proof. We shall try and explain why we present the Defence case. We are going to point to the erroneous strategy on the part of Prosecution, and we shall present a short overview of the evidence that we will present to prove our case that has already been put forth. When it comes to the burden of proof, Your Honour, we would like to remind everybody of the main principle of every criminal proceedings including this one. The burden of proof is on the Prosecutor. It is on the Prosecutor all the time. It is on the Prosecutor even during the presentation of the Defence case, which means our position is clear and founded in the law. It is up to the Prosecutor to prove the elements of the indictments in the sense they have been presented in the indictment. What is it that our client Mr. Boskoski has been charged with. Let us remind ourselves. By the Second Amended Indictment, Ljube Boskoski has been charged with failing to investigate and punish the perpetrators in the crime which are mentioned in the indictment and who were under his de jure and de facto control allegedly. This is item 11 of the indictment. In other words, Ljube Boskoski has not been charged perpetrating the acts himself, ordering them, or participating in their perpetration in any way. He has been charged with command responsibility. It is our position that the evidence that has been heard so far has not proved any such responsibility on part of Mr. Ljube Boskoski. The Defence will not go into the reasons which the Prosecutor was guided by when it issued the indictment against Ljube Boskoski. But when the indictment was issued, the Prosecutor took upon himself the burden of proof. The Prosecutor had the right to present his case in the way best suited and the Trial Chamber, in -- during the presentation of the Prosecutor's case, has allowed the Prosecutor to do exactly that. However, the Prosecutor had to be aware of the fact that he has to accept the consequences of his choice in the selection of evidence to be presented as well as the witnesses that would be called. We are convinced, Your Honours, that this Trial Chamber will honour the presumption of innocence of the accused and that the burden of proof, not for a single moment, will be passed on to him. In a case in which the consequences for the accused are very grave, for example, the responsibility for not taking measures to punish a crime of murder, the Prosecutor cannot hope that any omissions and lax in the evidence will compensate by the facts which are not part of the evidence. We are convinced, Your Honours, that the Prosecutor has not called certain witnesses because he was aware that by testifying, these witnesses might jeopardise his case. However, this can by no means be justification for the Prosecutor's actions. We would like to remind that you at the outset of this trial, we emphasised that the omission on the part of the Prosecutor to call the witnesses which are obviously in a position to provide relevant proof has to be taken in evaluating certain evidence. For example, there were no witnesses that could speak about the structure and competences in the Ministry of Interior, save for the lowest levels. There were no witness from the crime prevention police under which authority is undertaking measures in order to elucidate crimes and discover perpetrators. There were no judges who took part in the proceedings. If these and such witnesses had been called, the Defence believes that these witnesses would have proven the position of the Defence on the competences and responsibilities of the minister; and in that sense, they would have refuted the Prosecutor's allegations. Your Honours, the Defence does not doubt the honesty and the professional attitude of the Prosecutor that he has shown during the proceedings. All we're saying is that this was his strategy that he choice and the decision that he made. All this time the Prosecutor has believed that he can prove the charges. At the same time, avoiding witnesses that might provide positive testimony and relevant facts about the case, because the Prosecutor was aware that these very facts would have shaken his position and his strategy. The question arises here, Your Honours, why is it that the -- the Defence is presenting their case in the first place. Why are we calling the witnesses to start with? The reason is not that the Defence thinks that there is even the slightest need to present something new or to additionally explain the Defence case. It is also not because the Defence believes that the Prosecutor proved any relevant part of the indictment. The reason why we're presenting our case is not to establish the lack of responsibility of Mr. Boskoski because we believe that his alleged responsibility has not been proven during the Prosecution case. To the contrary, our position is that the Trial Chamber is already in the position to set Mr. Boskoski free and find him not guilty. The main reasons, Your Honour, for which we are calling viva voce witnesses for which we're presenting written statements and additional documents is to give the Trial Chamber additional evidence in addition to the evidence that we've heard with an even more solid foundation that will allow you, Your Honours, to find Mr. Boskoski not guilty based on the complete and adequate basis for such decision. In other words, we would like to repel even the little unclarity that the Prosecutor intentionally or unintentionally left hanging in the air with regard to some very important issues in this case. We believe that our evidence will provide a positive contribution towards the elucidation of these ambiguities in order to allow the Trial Chambers to make their decision. With that intention in mind, we will present a majority of the 92 bis statements because they are actually a repetition of the evidence that we have already heard. The previous position has decided the scope and the framework of the Defence case. Your Honours, we do not want to reopen the case and all the issues that has already been treated and that leave nothing to be said. Many parts of this case have already been considered in an adequate way, and the reputation of the same facts would not contribute to the establishment of truth and would not help the Trial Chamber to make their decision. We have chosen only the limited aspects of the Prosecutor's case. We have opted only for a few witnesses that we propose to be heard viva voce. There are numerous other witnesses who would have a lot to say about the same facts, but we fully believe and we hope that the witnesses that you're going to hear will allow you to look at the totality of the efforts and activities that were made not only on the part of the witnesses but also by other persons who will not have been called to testify. In other words, when you listen to the witnesses, you have to be aware of the fact that this will not be only their testimony but the picture of all the other numerous witnesses who, together with them, and independently of them, undertook numerous measures but they could not appear before the Trial Chamber in person. The Prosecutor's strategy on the criminal investigation and Mr. Boskoski's responsibility in view of the Defence was nothing more than knocking on a wrong door. Throughout the proceedings, the Prosecutor ascribes to Mr. Boskoski the responsibilities that were not truly his and he does that only because he was minister. One thing is already clear, and after the Defence case is over we believe it will become even more clear, and this is that the Prosecutor tries to append upon the minister the duties and responsibilities which were not truly his but rather the responsibilities of the judiciary or other persons and organs in the ministry. In other words, for the most of his case, the Prosecutor has been knocking on a wrong door. The Prosecutor believes that the duties of a minister equal the duties of the ministry, which does not have any foundation in the evidence, laws, or practices. Starting from these premises, I dare say that the Prosecutor has put his case completely wrongly. He alleges that the police is in charge in criminal investigation, including the Ljuboten case; although, it is abundantly clear that the investigation in any such case is at the responsibility of the judiciary. The erroneous thesis on which the Prosecutor based his case was assigning to the Ministry of Interior and especially a minister all those duties that they truly did not have under the law. The lack of understanding of the position and the mandate of the ministry has led the Prosecutor to a wrong trail. The minister is simply not a replacement for all those whose responsibilities are determined by the law, nor can he assume the responsibilities of other employees in the ministry. The position of the Prosecutor leads almost to the principle of the objective responsibility which could be defined in the following way. Because a certain person is a minister, and only because of that fact, he is responsible for everything. In other words, objective or strict responsibility is a completely different thing than the responsibility of a superior pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute. The objective responsibility would mean that a superior person may be proclaimed guilty because of the position that he was in and for the simple fact that his subordinate committed a crime. Luckily enough, the case law of this Tribunal is the best protection from any such attempt to define the responsibility of a superior. Your Honours, on this occasion, I would also like to say that the responsibility of a superior is not an obligation on the part of the superior to arrive at results. In other words, the responsibility of a superior person is not based on the result. If the superior person has undertaken the necessary and reasonable measures, irrespective of the fact whether they resulted in a -- discovering and punishing the perpetrator, still the duty has been properly done. Your Honours, before I start explaining the evidence that we intend to present, allow me to repeat some of the measures -- some of the measures that the Minister Boskoski undertook, and these measures arise from the Prosecutor's case. These measures were undertaken transparently and objectively, as can be seen from Exhibit 1D6. On the 12th and then on the 14th of August, the duty operation centre of the Ministry of Interior sector in Skopje informed the duty prosecutor and the judge on the events in Ljuboten on the presence of bodies in the village and, thus, performing his duty and handing the case over to -- into the hands of the judiciary. On the 13th of August, 2001, only one day after the event in the village and around the village of Ljuboten, Minister Boskoski set up a commission consisting of the most responsible persons in the Ministry of Interior and tasked them with investigating what had happened in Ljuboten and around it. Let me remind the Trial Chamber that this is Exhibit number P73. He personally approached the media and said publicly how important is the fact that the representatives of the court went to the site which arises from Exhibit P362. I will remind you of some of his words on the occasion, and I quote: "One of the basic questions or issues of today's meeting are the bodies of the five civilians which are still inaccessible to the Macedonian security forces so as to enable them to investigate and establish the cause of death." The organs of the ministry continued to monitor the security situation around the village. Upon the initiative of the minister, the ministry proposed exhumation and post-mortem which was beyond the duty of either the minister or the ministry, and this has been clearly shown in Exhibit P102. It arises from this exhibit that there was a clear intention on the part of the minister and the ministry to elucidate the facts and establish the circumstances that led to the death of these people in the village of Ljuboten. Your Honours, as you may have seen from the evidence, efforts were made to interview the villagers of Ljuboten. One of the exhibits that speaks to that fact is Exhibit number P104. Whatever he did, the minister informed the coordination body in the government, in order to keep them abreast of the events in Ljuboten. He submitted to the government the report that the commission composed of the most responsible persons drafted on the 4th of September, which is Exhibit number P378. As the minister responsible for the situation in his area, he informed the government about this report and the government of the Republic of Macedonia discussed that report and drew conclusions based on it. This is 1D134. He acted in keeping with the conclusions of the government, and he submitted his proposals to the Ministry of Defence. The crime technologists undertook measures that it was allowed to use upped the law and that the court asked for it to undertake. The ministry submitted its report to the office of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in Skopje. There was full cooperation with the international community. There were continued efforts to collect information under rather difficult conditions on the part of the UBK through their operative sources. The minister personally supported the independent work of the judiciary. The minister personally provided support to the work of this Tribunal which is all visible in the evidence 1D202 and at numerous other pieces of evidence. In answering questions about Ljuboten, the minister said, and I quote: "There's no dilemma with regard to this matter. We, the Macedonian police, were the first one to ask for an investigation to be done into Ljuboten, and you know only too well that the reason why there was no on-site inspection was the fact that armed groups in the village did not allow the investigative judge, the prosecutor, and the crime prevention police of the Republic of Macedonia, and I'm talking about three independent organs, to enter the village and to establish the real situation on the same day when the report had been received that the crimes had been committed; and if we have been able to do that, the whole situation would be different. Then he goes on to say: "Look, the public prosecutor is an independent institution and I don't want to interfere with its work." And, finally: "We respect the international Tribunal, and we shall do our utmost to reveal the crimes and to investigate all the crimes that have been committed in the territory of the Republic of Macedonia." The minister also established a commission that was in charge of receiving complaints with regard to the behaviour of the police towards the Albanian population. Your Honours, I have mentioned just a few, maybe some dozen pieces of evidence, of the hundreds that we've had an occasion to see before this Trial Chamber. Contrary to the allegation on the part of the Prosecutor that the investigation was false, the evidence has shown that all the possible and reasonable measures were taken, and no superior should be required to undertake things that are impossible to undertake. Our evidence will show that Minister Boskoski did everything that was possible under the circumstances that prevailed in the Republic of Macedonia in the year 2001 and 2002. The Prosecution came forth with another wrong argument, according to the view of the Defence. He knocked on the wrong door, introducing the question of disciplinary procedures and responsibility of the minister to carry out these procedures. When the case of responsibility for failure to carry out criminal procedure fell through for the Prosecution, he opened a new case. He shifted to the area of responsibility of the minister for failure to undertake disciplinary measures. This area best shows how inaccurate and almost artificial the case is, which is trying to be proved towards or against Minister Boskoski. The new approach of the Prosecution about the responsibility of the minister is not founded in law or in the evidence. Two of the five witnesses which the Defence is calling to testify viva voce will clarify the facts presented also during the course of the presentation of the Prosecution and, in particular, that the minister did not have the authorisation to undertake disciplinary procedure, that his authorisations were to appoint disciplinary commissions, appoint persons authorised to undertake the procedure, and reach a decision in the first instance after the procedure has been carried out and the proposal of this disciplinary commission. These witnesses will clarify that a disciplinary procedure can be led only against people employed in the Ministry of Interior. And, Your Honours, as seeking responsibility for the ministry in the criminal procedure fell under the weight and force of the evidence, also the theory for alleged responsibility of the minister because of failure to undertake disciplinary measures be also, once again, knocking on the wrong door. Allow me now, Your Honours, to turn, in short, to the evidence which the Defence will present in the upcoming period. Witness number 2, on the 65 ter list of the Defence, will give testimony viva voce. In this case, in which the Minister of the Interior is accused, the Prosecutor decided not to call any experts from the area of the internal affairs, especially experts that could speak about the structure and work of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Macedonia. We believe that from that fact the Trial Chamber can have the wrong conclusions. What is important for us is that witness number 2 can provide positive, relevant proof that will assist the Trial Chamber to better understand the laws and the practice that determined the behaviour of the minister and which are of importance for this case. This testimony, from the point of view of an expert, will be a confirmation of the statements of credible and reliable witnesses presented already before this Court. The expert witness will, among other things, clarify the following: The place and structure of the Ministry of Interior in the legal system of the Republic of Macedonia in its relation with other state bodies; explain the function of the Ministry of Interior and how the work and responsibilities are allocated and organised in the Ministry of Interior, both horizontally and vertically; explain who, in accordance with the law of the employees of the ministries which is of importance for establishing issues of his responsibility in the disciplinary procedure; explain why reservists are not subject to disciplinary procedures. The topic of his expertise will be the notion -- the term of authorised person. What this means from the point of view of authorisations and powers in terms of duties and activities in the Ministry of Interior. The expert witness will clarify also the role of the minister in terms of the work of the ministry with a particular view to the role of including the MOI or the role of the MOI in the investigation activities and disciplinary procedure, will clarify the role of the MOI in the criminal procedure when the Ministry of Interior is under the authority of judicial bodies. He will also clarify that the minister does not have a role nor authorities in this procedure. The expert, Your Honours, will also clarify the role of those bodies of the ministries which do have certain tasks in the pre-criminal and criminal investigation, and will list who and when has certain authorisations over them. The witness will clarify also why the competences and authorisations which the Prosecution claims to be of the minister are, in effect, not his. The expert will show that the minister is not an operative part in the activities of the Ministry of Interior. He will clarify the law and the functioning operation of the disciplinary procedure in the MOI and, in particular, the role of the minister in this process. Contrary to the claims of the Prosecution, the expert will show that the minister cannot and does not have the authorisation to initiate a disciplinary procedure in the Ministry of Interior. The expert witness will also give his expertise about two other issues which are relevant to this case: The nature and the specific characteristics of individual commissions, such as the up with which Minister Boskoski set up for examining the case of Ljuboten; and on other issue, the relevance of the law on Amnesty after the procedure of the MOI. In accordance with presenting the evidence of the expert witness, the Trial Chamber can also debate other relevant issues, positions of the minister. It will be confirmed that the role of the Ministry of Interior is no different than the roles of ministers in other ministries. The nature of authorities in ministry changes but not the position and the responsibility of the minister. He is a manager with precise authorisations as are ministers of foreign affairs, culture, information, and others, which clearly derives from this Law on State Administration. This is exhibit P92, Articles 47 to 49. This will show that the role of the minister derives from the law, stems from the law, and that the Minister of Interior cannot be put on the same level as the commander of the army of the Republic of Macedonia at any which time. The expert will show that the minister does not replace other bodies and individuals in the MOI, that he is not a police officer, a commander, an inspector in operative sectors. He is not a director of the state security service or another sector. The minister is a minister with his own rights and responsibilities. Witness, under the number 1, from the 65 ter list of the Defence witnesses, will be called because he can testify about some crucial issues of this case. The Defence feels that the testimony of this witness is relevant to establish the following. Contrary to the claims of the Prosecution, the minister, in accordance with the regulations of the Republic of Macedonia, does not have the obligation or authorisation to undertake a disciplinary procedure. Contrary to the claims of the Prosecution, the role of the minister in the disciplinary procedure is limited to appointing members of the disciplinary commissions, appointing persons authorised to undertake such procedures, and passing decisions on the proposal of the disciplinary commissions after the established procedure has been carried out. Contrary to the allegations and claims of the Prosecution, the decision of the minister in the disciplinary procedure is not final. It can be changed in the appeal procedure from the disciplinary commission in the government or in a judicial procedure. Thus, this witness will show that the minister does not initiate nor does it end the disciplinary procedure. Contrary to the claims of the Prosecution, the witness will show that a disciplinary procedure cannot be led against reservists. Contrary to the claims of the Prosecution, persons suspect for having committed criminal acts in and around Ljuboten, if they were not employed of the MOI or unless they were employees of the MOI, could not have been subject to a disciplinary procedure in the MOI. The Defence expects that the witness, in the course of his testimony, to present the following. That only persons employed in the Ministry of Interior, persons against whom a disciplinary procedure can be led. Disciplinary procedure is regulated by law on the Ministry of Interior, collective agreements, other by-laws and decisions of the minister. The witness is fully aware of the system, the rules, and procedures in view of the professional experience and long-term practice on legal issues in the Ministry of Interior. These laws and by-laws, in full, are determined by the bodies and regulate the procedure under which a disciplinary procedure is carried out. The regulations also lay out the sanctions and the manner in which the procedure is implemented if various regulations -- in various cases foreseen by regulations. We expect that the witness will explain which conditions must be fulfilled in order for a person to become an employee of the MOI, will clarify also the special conditions which an employee must fulfil in order to be employed in the Ministry of Interior. We believe that the witness will also testify about the appeal procedure on the decision of the ministers which takes place in front of the government commission, which has its own rules of procedure. Also, as we, in deciding to call this witness, said we anticipate that this witness will confirm that the minister does not have the right to initiate a disciplinary procedure and that reservists cannot be subject to this procedure. In his testimony, we expect the witness to show that in this procedure in front of the commission, which carries out the evidence and assesses responsibility, the minister does not have any role at all. The minister will -- the witness will also show that the disciplinary procedure can be led only against known individuals for breaking the disciplinary, and this follows very swiftly. The role of the minister in the disciplinary procedure, we expect, will be confirmed by this witness and that he will confirm that the minister can only reach a decision about appointing members of the commission, to appoint persons responsible for initiating the procedure, and to reach a decision on the proposal of the disciplinary commission after this procedure has been carried out. Also, he will clarify that this decision of the minister can be appealed, that will be decided by an independent government commission, and a judicial case can also be led against such a case of the minister. The witness number 3, on the 65 ter list, is called because the Defence believes the witness can provide relevant and reliable facts to the Court -- to the Trial Chamber. This witness, as well as others, will be called due to previously listed reasons for calling witnesses, but his testimony is specifically linked, in addition to the already listed, to the testimony of witness M-052. It is clear that already in the process of cross-examination, the Defence raised the issue of the credibility of Witness M-052 and the truthfulness and reliability of the information which Witness M-052 presented before this Court. In his testimony, the witness attempted to present his own activities as responsibility of others who gave orders to him. We claim that this person transfers responsibility to others because it is not in a position to justify his own activities and undertake responsibility for the own work within the framework of his own duties. The receipt of the statement of this witness without giving the Trial Chamber the opportunity to re-examine the statement by way of other witnesses would seriously endanger the integrity of this trial. The witness who we are calling was, during the time and events and relates to Witness M-052, can present facts contrary to the allegations of witness M-052 and can, in fact, present the facts as they did occur. Contrary to Witness M-052, the witness comes without any promise of any kind, without any deals, without any discussions of these deals which could be offered to a witness. In addition, the witness comes fully aware and with the knowledge that the Prosecution will accuse him that he was a member of a joint criminal enterprise. This witness, as well as Mr. Bliznakovski, according to the Prosecution, are members of joint criminal enterprise due to one reason alone, because of the testimony of witness M-052 which this one gave to the Prosecution and which the Prosecution called aware that this witness is not speaking the truth. The witness accepted to testify not in order to explain his own role but to give an accurate statement about what he and the others actually did. Your Honours, you will maybe conclude that what this witness did was imperfect, but you will have in front of you an honourable and honest police officer who did the best he could in the given circumstances. Apart from this, this witness, as we stated in the data about his testimony, will testify to the structure and the competences of the sectors of internal affairs and departments of internal affairs, SVR and OVR. He will also speak about the participation of the Ministry of Interior in the pre-trial stage of the procedure, about the tasks of the MOI in the course of the criminal investigation, about the time and the entities who submit a criminal report, and about other issues indicated in the summary of his testimony. The Witness number 4, from the 65 ter list of the Defence, will testify contrary to the assertion of the Prosecutor that the measures that Boskoski undertook were inadequate and ill-intended, that it was a sham investigation. The testimony of this witness will show that the measures that Minister Boskoski undertook were in good faith to fully clarify the situation in and around Ljuboten, and that measures are taken against any perpetrators. Contrary to the assertions of the Prosecutor, he never agreed nor approved the crimes committed in and around Ljuboten, if any. Contrary to the contention of the Prosecutor, Minister Boskoski also demonstrated personal interest in clarifying the situation around Ljuboten. Contrary to the assertion of the Prosecutor, this testimony, as well, will show that the Minister Boskoski informed the justice system bodies, especially the prosecutor, about all findings that the minister came across. So, with this in mind, we expect that the witness will testify that the Minister Boskoski requested that information related to Ljuboten are collected. I apologise. That he undertook measures to come to those information from various sources: Bodies of the Ministry of Interior, sectors for internal affairs of Skopje, department of internal affairs, forensic police department, forensics medicine institute. This witness also participated in the meetings, and he transferred all the materials collected to the public Prosecutor. Witness could assist the Chamber to decide whether the information that the MOI had were communicated to the justice system bodies, especially to the Prosecutor. The Witness number 5, in the 65 ter list, will testify in a similar way as to witness before him. The relevance of this testimony is similar to the relevance of the testimony of the witness that I just spoke about. The truth and the testimony of this witness comprises the period after the time indicated in the indictment, but it demonstrates the continuous efforts of Minister Boskoski and the ministry to fully elucidate the events in and around Ljuboten and to undertake appropriate measures. So this testimony contradicts the assertion of the Prosecutor that the measures that Minister Boskoski undertook were inadequate and ill-intended. The Defence believes that this witness will be important to ascertain that Minister Boskoski acted in good faith, intending that the issues around Ljuboten are elucidated, that Minister Boskoski does not agree or approve of the crime regardless of who was the perpetrator of it, that Minister Boskoski demonstrated personal interest to clarify all and any crimes, including the crimes, if any, committed in and around Ljuboten. What this witness can testify to are the efforts of the task force that he belonged to, to obtain as many information as possible about any crime committed. The witness will testify about the measures that he personally undertook to learn what happened in and around Ljuboten. He will also testify to the involvement of numerous bodies in the efforts to clarify, elucidate the crimes that took place in the Republic of Macedonia. His testimony will shed additional light to the overall efforts undertaken in and outside the ministry in order to clarify the events in and around Ljuboten. The witness will testify also why he and the members of the task force were unable to do more than that. Your Honours, the Defence proposed that 11 witness will testify according to the 92 bis rule, that they are not called to testify before the Court, and that their testimonies are accepted in writing as written statements. The testimonies of these witnesses are a vehicle through which Defence offers the Chamber the necessary facts related to the context in which the events described in the indictment transpired. Apart from this, some of the proposed statements will enable the Trial Chamber to assess the reliability of the testimonies of a number of Prosecutor's witnesses, the reliability of whom was questioned during their testimony. Some of these statements corroborate earlier evidence about the involvement of the president of the Republic of Macedonia in the events around Ljuboten, as well as the fact that numerous persons regarding which the Prosecutor asserts that they were at Ljuboten never really became members of the MOI. A part of the 92 bis statements speaks about the personality of Minister Boskoski. All evidence tendered will show that it is simply impossible to conclude that Minister Boskoski failed to take all possible and reasonable measures that he had the duty to undertake in the given circumstances. At the end, Your Honours, I wish to say the following: At this moment, many people in the Republic of Macedonia are following the work of this Chamber with due attention. Many people in Macedonia are asking today the question whether this Chamber will really try the case on the basis of evidence and whether it will really require that the Prosecutor must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. This Defence, the person we appear for, Mr. Boskoski, and I personally, have faith in the international legal system and in this Court. In the light of the evidence that you heard and those that you will hear, I am convinced that you will be able to bring the only just decision in this case. The Defence believes that you will acquit Mr. Boskoski, based on the counts of the indictment, for the simple reason that you will be convinced that he is not responsible for the actions that he is accused of. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Residovic. Mr. Apostolski, were you considering making an opening statement at this point, or would you prefer to do so after the close of the evidence led for the Defence of Mr. Boskoski? I think the Rules would allow you to take either course.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence of Mr. Johan Tarculovski will make its opening statement before the start of leading of evidence of Defence of Mr. Johan Tarculovski, so after the Defence of Mr. Boskoski has led its evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, as the opening statement of the Defence of Mr. Boskoski has now been given by Ms. Residovic, according to the timetable proposed, the Chamber will now adjourn, with a view to commencing hearing the witnesses to be called by the Defence of Mr. Boskoski, commencing tomorrow morning at 9.00. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 31st day of January, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.07 a.m.,
